documents.abstract: Transformers can implement reinforcement-learning algorithms in context, yet how off-policy control emerges within Transformers remains poorly understood. We study Q-learning, a foundational model-free control algorithm that combines off-policy bootstrapping with greedy policy improvement. We prove that a two-layer attention-only Transformer can implement a finite-temperature form of Q-learning, where the temperature $τ>0$ controls the approximation to greedy action selection, recovering window Q-learning as $τ\to0$. We train the structured Transformer on randomly generated MDP tasks using output-only supervision. Experiments show that the theoretically predicted parameter structure emerges during training, including the internal greedy action-selection mechanism, and that the trained Transformer achieves performance comparable to Q-learning on unseen tasks. Our theoretical analysis further shows that the equivalent realizations form a solution manifold and that, under suitable task-diversity conditions, the training iterates converge locally to this manifold at an exponential rate. For the random-task model analyzed here, the local worst-case number of gradient steps needed to reduce the distance to the manifold by a factor $ε$ is $Θ\left(τ^{-5}\log(1/\varepsilon)\right)$, quantifying the increasing optimization cost as the learned update approaches window Q-learning.

Large language models rely on prompt context to perform in-context learning, follow formats, and adapt to local evidence. This ability, however, also raises a robustness concern: models may reuse irrelevant tokens from earlier context when answering a later query. Prior work identifies this behavior as contextual entrainment and finds attention heads whose ablation reduces it, arguing that these heads are largely task- or relation-specific. But are the mechanisms behind contextual entrainment truly isolated by relation, or do relation-conditioned searches recover reusable components shared across relations? Using factual-distractor relation-completion prompts across 19 lexical-semantic subtypes, we identify attention heads whose ablation reduces entrainment and test how the resulting head sets transfer recovery ability across exact relations, semantic families, and mixed relation distributions. Same-family transfer exceeds different-family transfer, family residuals weaken once globally shared heads are removed, and subtype-specific searches repeatedly rediscover many global heads. Clean-completion and context-use probes further suggest that this shared intervention can reduce harmful copying while preserving ordinary relation completion and simple in-context abilities. Our findings provide a more precise perspective on contextual entrainment and its mitigation: harmful context following is not best addressed by searching for isolated relation-specific circuits, but by using heterogeneous attack prompts to reveal reusable intervention targets whose effects are shaped by semantic relation structure.

This study presents a convergent mixed-methods empirical investigation of user perceptions of Virtual Heritage Mentors (VHMs) in AI-mediated intangible cultural heritage learning. The study draws on an online survey of 370 participants and semi-structured interviews with 20 independently recruited participants, all of whom were ethnically Chinese. The results indicated that participants prioritized interactive explanation, clarification, and guided support over visual realism. Trust was associated with cultural accuracy, contextual grounding, transparency, and respect for heritage communities. Emotional resonance was valued less as anthropomorphic simulation than as pedagogical care expressed through patience, encouragement, re-explanation, and responsiveness. Participants also envisioned VHMs as adaptive learning companions while emphasizing that AI should complement rather than replace human practitioners. These findings empirically support and refine the proposed VHM framework by highlighting relational mediation, relational mentorship, co-transmission, and human–AI complementarity as key design priorities. The study argues for shifting digital heritage design from representation alone toward relational, culturally accountable support for heritage learning and transmission.

Abstract In the last four decades, the transmission of a live surgical operation to a remote audience has evolved from closed-circuit educational broadcast into a fully remote, robot-assisted surgery performed across different continents. This review maps that journey systematically, defining a six-rung Digital Surgical Spectrum — from passive live broadcast to artificial-intelligence-augmented autonomous surgery — grounding each stage in published clinical evidence across multiple surgical domains. We demonstrate that each rung of this spectrum is no longer theoretical. Live broadcasts have reached audiences across multiple countries. Tele-proctoring was validated at scale during the COVID-19 pandemic, and tele-mentoring has been shown in systematic review to produce a safety and efficacy profile broadly comparable to on-site supervision. True remote tele-surgery has been accomplished over distances exceeding 8,000 km with latencies well within established procedure specific safety thresholds. We also present a case timeline and an Institutional Readiness Framework specifying the technical, regulatory, and other prerequisites for each rung, organized visually as a Digital Surgical Spectrum. Importantly, nuances such as the performance paradox of observed surgery, consent frameworks, cybersecurity risk, regulatory fragmentation, and the threat of entrenching rather than correcting global surgical inequity are examined. As the field advances, the growth of tele-surgical technologies will depend on international regulatory harmonization and equity-centered deployment, supported by prospective multi-specialty outcome registries.

The integration of generative artificial intelligence into contemporary artistic practices requires reconsidering creativity, authorship, and originality, transforming relationships between artist, tool, and artwork. Unlike conventional digital technologies, which execute operations defined by creators, generative systems exhibit operational autonomy, producing partly unpredictable visual configurations. This raises questions about algorithmic intervention and the possibility of attributing co-authorship to artificial intelligence systems. This article examines the relationship between human creators and generative technologies through computational creativity, distributed authorship, and philosophical perspectives on nonhuman agency. It distinguishes systems’ operational autonomy from artists’ intentional autonomy, arguing that algorithmic participation does not necessarily imply creative subjectivity comparable to human experience. It also examines the aesthetic and conceptual implications of human–machine collaboration and the reorganisation of artistic practices through generation, selection, interpretation, and post-production. The study argues that generative artificial intelligence reconfigures human authorship, shifting creative activity from direct execution toward intention formulation, system configuration, and critical evaluation. Artists therefore retain a decisive role in directing the process and taking responsibility for its artistic outcomes. Algorithmic co-authorship serves as a conceptual tool for understanding these emerging production relationships, without implying legal authorship or artificial consciousness.

This article examines the theoretical and methodological aspects of optimizing treasury business processes through artificial intelligence and machine learning technologies. It substantiates the need for treasury digitalization to move beyond converting processes into electronic form towards the intelligent use of data. The article proposes a decision-support mechanism based on analyzing digital process traces through Process Mining, identifying redundant and repetitive operations, intelligently automating standard low-risk operations, and generating forecasts using machine learning. The author develops G-TOP, a mechanism for the intelligent optimization of treasury business processes, and TIOI, the Treasury Intelligent Optimization Index, to evaluate its effectiveness. The research findings demonstrate that artificial intelligence should be used in treasury operations not as a substitute for human decision-making, but as a technology that improves the quality of decisions

documents.abstract: Gender research in vocational education has primarily examined women’s exclusion, while male students’ experiences of privilege and masculinity-related pressure remain underexplored. This study examined how male vocational students experienced gender-based privilege, encountered psychological and pedagogical burdens, and interpreted their relationship during manufacturing internships. The study employed a qualitative design informed by a constructivist–interpretivist paradigm and Masculinity Studies, particularly Connell’s relational approach to masculinities. The study analyzed semi-structured interviews with 61 male students from two vocational secondary schools in Bekasi, Indonesia, using reflexive thematic analysis. Participants reported that gendered expectations associating men with strength, readiness, courage, and independence facilitated early access to core technical tasks, supervisory trust, and valuable learning opportunities. The same expectations intensified performance demands, physical workloads, risk exposure, restricted help-seeking, and limited pedagogical support. Participants interpreted this position through normalization, ambivalence, and critical reflection. Some proposed competency-based task allocation, equitable supervision, and safer learning environments. The study introduces conditional access privilege as a gendered position in which access to valuable technical learning resources must be maintained through masculine performance, generating psychological pressure and pedagogical vulnerability. The findings support internship practices that separate competency assessment, task allocation, supervision, and learning support from gendered expectations.

Research on gender-related online content is often operationalized through harm-centered tasks that collapse non-harmful gender-related and unrelated content, while existing datasets remain concentrated in high-resource languages and Global North settings. To bridge these gaps, we introduce GENDIS, a dataset of 9,600 multilingual, human-annotated YouTube comments from India, Kenya, and Nigeria (3,200 per country), annotated using a two-level framework that first identifies whether gender is referenced and then classifies gender-related content as negative, positive, or neutral. This separation provides a denominator for gender-related discourse independent of harm, enabling both prevalence estimation and characterization of its evaluative range. In the uniform random stratum, 23.8-35.0% of comments are gender-related, and among those with a resolved stance, 82% are neutral or positive. Across models, gender-reference detection is substantially easier than stance classification, especially for positive and neutral speech. Lightly supervised classifiers match frontier zero-shot large language models at substantially lower cost and outperform generic toxicity detection, while cross-country transfer remains limited. GENDIS provides a locally grounded resource for measuring when gender is invoked online and how that reference is framed.

documents.abstract: Rapid integration of generative artificial intelligence (AI) into enterprise processes highlights critical gaps in workforce readiness in terms of skills required for successful implementation of new technologies. This paper introduces a framework which will enable use of generative AI for conducting dynamic skill gap analysis and providing personalized recommendations for upskilling. The framework includes mapping of competencies according to shifting role demands, individual performance assessment through AI and adaptation of learning path for each individual based on results. Using the information obtained from surveys about AI adoption in enterprises and competency maps developed in recent research, this paper will show how generative AI can be used for making static learning programs adaptive and relevant to the current needs of learners. The problem discussed in the paper is related to not only technical AI literacy, but also to human skills, such as critical thinking, ethical decision-making and change management. Comparative analysis of methods shows that personalized training offered by generative AI is more engaging and relevant than generic models of training programs.

This study examines the role of generative artificial intelligence in detecting corporate greenwashing during periods of climate shock. The main objective is to analyze to what extent generative AI tools improve the identification of discrepancies between companies' environmental discourse and their actual environmental performance. The analysis is based on an international panel of listed companies from sectors highly exposed to climate risks over the period 2000–2025. The methodology combines dynamic panel econometric techniques, machine learning models and natural language processing approaches based on generative AI to detect narrative and semantic inconsistencies associated with greenwashing. The results show that climate shocks significantly increase greenwashing practices, while generative AI models substantially improve the accuracy and speed of their detection. The effects are particularly pronounced in carbon-intensive industries and in weakly regulated institutional environments.

The increasing integration of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) in English language teaching calls for an immediate and thorough response from language teachers. Employing an exploratory qualitative approach, the study explores how 10 English language instructors at a Chinese university integrate GenAI tools in language teaching through lesson study. Data were collected through classroom observations, recordings of collaborative lesson preparation/reflection sessions, teaching materials, and three rounds of in-depth interviews. Our analysis centres on the transformative impact of GenAI on teachers’ digital literacy practices, conceptualised as doing, meaning, relating, thinking, and “being.” The study contrasted the participants’ new digital literacy practices with their previous practices in various professional practice domains and traced the sustainability of these practices over time. Findings reveal that GenAI catalysed a transformation of teachers’ practices across lesson planning, instruction, and assessment. However, the sustainability of these practices varied due to multiple factors. We argue that sustainable GenAI integration requires viewing digital literacy as a situated social practice shaped by utility and professional risk. The study offers insights for developing collaborative professional development programmes that support teachers’ critical and sustainable engagement with GenAI.

Establishing the chief complaint requires identifying the patient’s main symptoms or concerns. This information is essential for triage and subsequent clinical assessment. However, patients may struggle to describe their symptoms or leave important concerns unspoken. Also, clinicians have limited time to ask further questions during intake. Generative AI could help by asking patients what is troubling them, when their symptoms began, and what other concerns they have. It could prepare a short summary for patients to correct and clinicians to review. Clinical studies of AI-assisted intake have reported shorter physician consultations and more complete recorded histories. These findings do not show whether AI helps clinicians establish the chief complaint more accurately. We propose an evaluation framework centered on the proportion of patients whose main symptoms or concerns are missing or incorrectly described after AI-assisted intake. Studies should compare what patients wanted to discuss with what the AI agent asked about and included in its summary. They should also examine whether concerns requiring urgent assessment were missed. The clinical goal is a clear description of the patient’s main symptoms and concerns that helps clinicians judge urgency and decide what needs attention.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is creating new possibilities for distance education through conversational learning support, personalised explanations, automated feedback and multilingual assistance. However, its integration also raises concerns regarding academic integrity, unequal access, information reliability, learner autonomy and data privacy. This paper develops a conceptual framework for integrating GenAI into distance education through a human-in-the-loop approach. Drawing on relevant scholarly literature and international educational policy documents, the study examines the relationship between AI-supported personalisation, inclusive learning, human oversight and academic accountability. It proposes an integrated framework in which teachers and learners retain meaningful decision-making authority while AI provides supplementary educational support. The framework comprises five dimensions: human agency, equitable access, learner-centred personalisation, academic integrity and responsible data governance. The paper argues that technological availability alone cannot guarantee educational improvement; effective implementation also requires AI literacy, appropriate assessment practices, institutional policies and continuous human evaluation. The proposed framework offers conceptual guidance for higher-education institutions seeking to adopt GenAI responsibly in distance-learning environments. As a conceptual contribution, it requires subsequent empirical evaluation to establish its applicability across different educational contexts.

documents.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is reshaping digital marketing by enabling personalised, scalable, and innovative content, while simultaneously raising concerns regarding authenticity and consumer trust. This study examines how Perceived Authenticity, Perceived Personalization, and Perceived Usefulness/Innovation influence Brand Perception and Purchase Intention among Generation Z consumers, with Brand Perception serving as a mediating mechanism. A quantitative, cross-sectional research design was employed using data from 425 Generation Z consumers collected through a structured questionnaire based on five-point Likert-type scales. The data were analysed using descriptive statistics, reliability analysis, Pearson and Spearman correlations, multiple regression, variance inflation factors, HC3 robust standard errors, and bootstrapped mediation analysis based on 5,000 resamples. The findings indicate that Perceived Authenticity (β = .234), Perceived Personalization (β = .160), and Perceived Usefulness/Innovation (β = .407) significantly and positively influence Brand Perception. Brand Perception significantly predicts Purchase Intention (β = .520). Significant indirect effects were observed for Perceived Authenticity (β = .122), Perceived Personalization (β = .083), and Perceived Usefulness/Innovation (β = .212) through Brand Perception. The findings demonstrate that consumer responses to GenAI marketing translate into purchase intention substantially through broader brand evaluations. The study highlights the importance of combining AI-enabled innovation and personalization with authenticity and consistent brand positioning.
topics: Consumer Behavior in Brand Consumption and Identification

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly embedded in students’ learning and knowledge-work routines, yet perceived productivity gains do not necessarily arise from technology acceptance alone. This study develops and empirically examines an integrated Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and Self-Regulated Learning (SRL) framework for explaining learning productivity among Google/Gemini users in Bangladesh. The study dataset contains 400 respondent IDs, of which 385 records contain complete questionnaire responses and a valid attention-check response; 15 rows are blank. The analysis therefore uses 385 usable cases and conducts an additional sensitivity analysis on 302 respondents classified as regular or occasional AI-feature users. Perceived ease of use (PEOU), perceived usefulness (PU), SRL and learning productivity (LP) were operationalised using three five-point Likert items each. Transparent composite-score path analysis with 5,000 bootstrap resamples was used because the available analytical environment did not contain a dedicated CFA/PLS-SEM implementation; consequently, the reported measurement diagnostics are explicitly treated as pre-publication validation evidence rather than as a claim of completed covariance-based CFA or PLS-SEM. PEOU positively predicted PU (β = .278, p < .001), while both PEOU (β = .191, p < .001) and PU (β = .218, p < .001) predicted SRL. Learning productivity was predicted by PEOU (β = .140, p = .004), PU (β = .256, p < .001) and SRL (β = .202, p < .001), with R² = .188. Bootstrap estimates also supported indirect pathways from PEOU to LP through PU and SRL, including a serial PEOU → PU → SRL → LP effect. The results suggest that the productivity value of GenAI is partly behavioural: users benefit not only because the technology is perceived as useful and easy to operate, but also because those perceptions are associated with planning, monitoring and addressing learning gaps. The study contributes an emerging-market, mechanism-oriented account of GenAI-enabled learning productivity and identifies measurement and sampling issues that should be resolved in subsequent validation research.

Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) can reduce the time and cognitive effort required for university learning, yet technical efficiency does not necessarily translate into improved student well-being. This article develops and tests a conversion account of this paradox by distinguishing efficiency gains that remain available as student-controlled resources from gains that are associated with perceived increases in performance expectations, competitive pressure, verification work, and dependence. A sequential three-study mixed-methods program was conducted with undergraduates in Jiangxi Province. Study 1 used codebook thematic analysis of 42 interviews to identify six mechanisms linking immediate efficiency to resource retention or perceived pressure. Study 2 surveyed 1268 students across eight universities. GenAI use was strongly associated with perceived efficiency gains, but also with perceived performance-standard escalation and verification burden. Positive retention and negative competition pathways were similar in magnitude, yielding a nonsignificant total association with well-being; working-time retention strengthened the efficiency–well-being association. Because Study 2 was cross-sectional, these pathways are interpreted as indirect associations rather than causal mediation. Study 3 used a 2 × 2 experiment (N = 320) and found that AI access improved task quality and reduced completion time under both performance-norm conditions, whereas gains in autonomy, retained time, and state well-being were evident under the stable norm but not statistically distinguishable from zero under the escalated norm. The findings distinguish technical affordance from context-dependent conversion and suggest that responsible AI integration should consider whether efficiency gains remain available for learning, recovery, and student-directed use alongside productivity.

Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used to support programming education, but its use in learning-from-errors activities has received limited research attention. This quasi-experimental study compared AI-guided and human-guided support in a structured learning-from-errors programming activity, focusing on students’ perceptions and their variability. A total of 59 college students completed the JavaScript error-detection and correction activity under AI-guided or human-guided support. Following the activity, students completed a questionnaire measuring perceived learning experience, satisfaction, general motivation, self-regulated learning (SRL), and self-efficacy. Between-group differences were examined using Mann–Whitney U tests, and differences in variability were examined using Levene’s tests. Students in the AI-guided condition reported significantly more positive learning experiences and greater satisfaction than those in the human-guided condition. They also reported significantly higher overall SRL and greater use of SRL strategies. No significant differences were found in general motivation, SRL motivation, SRL planning and organization, or self-efficacy. The AI-guided group showed significantly lower raw variability in satisfaction and self-efficacy. However, a sensitivity analysis did not establish that these variance differences remained after accounting for mean-related constraints on the bounded response scale. The findings suggest that GenAI may serve as a scaffold for error analysis when integrated in ways that maintain students’ active cognitive engagement.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: This project documents the methods and analytical framework of a scoping review examining how generative artificial intelligence is used to support learning and research competency development among postgraduate nursing students. The review focuses on six competency domains: information literacy and evidence retrieval, evidence-based practice competency, research methodology and analytical skills, academic writing and scientific communication, critical thinking and research thinking, and AI literacy and responsible AI use. Study selection and data charting were completed before OSF registration; therefore, the registration is intended to provide a transparent record of the review methods rather than a prospective preregistration.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming higher education, influencing how students learn, produce knowledge, and engage in assessments. This study examines the ethical implications of AI integration in university courses and its perceived impact on students’ cognitive skills. Using a mixed-methods secondary data analysis, survey data from 23,218 students across 109 countries and 252 teachers from China, Romania, India, and Brunei were analyzed to explore perceptions of AI capabilities, ethical boundaries, behavioral intentions, and cognitive outcomes. The results have shown that although students are aware of the potential of AI in improving the efficiency and content creation and assistance in the learning process, there are still concerns about overdependence, plagiarism, and lack of critical thinking. The views of faculty underline moral direction and the necessity of systematic assimilation. Developing upon these insights, a theoretical framework is developed that connects antecedent variables, behavior intentions and institutional context to two outcomes the cognitive impact and institutional influence. This framework offers a guide on how universities should introduce generative AI in a responsible manner, and strike a balance between ethical principles and training higher-order cognitive abilities.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI
Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Activation steering controls large language models at inference time, but its effectiveness depends on the choice of reference data. We introduce genesis steering, which derives a genesis vector from contrastive examples in the model's own fine-tuning data. When these data are unavailable, we draw on the membership inference literature to identify likely training examples and construct a proxy dataset. We establish two theoretical results on optimal displacement to the decision boundary and reduced proxy-estimation bias. We evaluate genesis steering and membership-based proxy construction on Tülu-3-8B, whose fine-tuning data are publicly available, and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct as a control. We find that safety data from Tülu-3-8B's training mixture yield stronger steering than external datasets on both models. On Tülu-3-8B, membership scores largely agree in identifying training examples, and vectors built from top-ranked examples achieve competitive performance against random subsets of the same size. In contrast, the results on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct hint that a MIA method will only have a positive effect if the mean direction shift with MIA-filtered in-distribution data is much less severe than the direction shift with OoD data.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) struggle with metric and multi-view relationships that remain implicit in RGB observations. Geometry foundation models recover this structure from RGB, but existing methods either fuse the estimated features with visual tokens and learn to use them from question answering alone, or align VLM latents with geometry features. Capturing geometry, however, does not ensure its use: zeroing the aligned latents of a released feature-alignment model leaves its accuracy unchanged. We introduce GeoReader, a framework that learns geometric representations for the VLM that reads them. First, we train lightweight Geometric Readers to produce continuous input tokens, supervising them with geometry descriptions decoded by a frozen VLM, so that the Readers express geometry in a form the target model can already read. We then freeze the Readers to preserve this interface while fine-tuning the VLM on spatial QA, with geometry injection conditioned on the question. Geometry descriptions serve only as training targets: at inference, the VLM answers directly from the continuous geometric tokens without generating a geometry chain of thought. With geometry predicted from RGB images, our approach reaches 94.3 on MindCube-Tiny with Qwen3-VL-4B and, with a multi-source QA mixture, an average of 72.5 across six additional spatial benchmarks with Qwen3.5-9B. These results suggest that a useful geometric representation is one the receiving model can use, not merely one from which geometry can be reconstructed.

A Geotechnical Instrumentation Plan defines the objectives, scope, and methodology for monitoring the behavior of the ground and structures to manage risk throughout a mining project. Its purpose is to translate a site’s hazard and performance criteria into a targeted array of sensors, data collection procedures, alarm thresholds, and response actions. This chapter details a step-by-step process for creating a site-specific instrumentation plan, from initial site investigation and failure-mode analysis to instrument selection, siting, and data protocols. Key elements are discussed in depth: identification of monitoring goals, selection of parameters and sensor t ypes, spatial density and redundancy requirements, and determination of sampling frequency. We outline the contents of an Operation, Maintenance, and Surveillance (OMS) manual, including roles and responsibilities, data protocols, alarm matrices, and escalation procedures (with example tables). Worked design examples illustrate instrument spacing and telemetry design calculations with equations. Comparative tables recommend instrument choices for common scenarios (open-pit walls, underground workings, tailings dams, mine rail). Guidance is provided on procurement, installation, commissioning, and verification of instruments, as well as data management, cybersecurity, and archival practices. Cost and complexity considerations are addressed qualitatively. Three concise case studies (e.g., tailings dam incidents) highlight practical lessons. Finally, common pitfalls and mitigation strategies are summarized, and checklists/templates are presented in table form for field teams. This chapter emphasizes standards-based practice: International Council on Mining and Metals (ICMM’s) Global Tailings Standard and Good Practice Guide call for rigorous site-specific monitoring plans. Throughout, we cite recent official and scholarly sources to support the guidance.

Universities promote generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) as a pedagogical resource while regulating it as a risk to academic integrity and fair assessment. This study examines how differentiated policy framing varies across substantive policy dimensions and national contexts, and how students interpret and navigate such guidance in practice. Using a convergent mixed-methods design with quantitative priority, we analyzed GenAI policy documents from 36 universities in Denmark, the United Kingdom, the United States, and the Netherlands, complemented by eight semi-structured interviews with graduate students at one sampled university. Aspect-based sentiment analysis and mixed-effects modeling show significantly positive sentiment in teaching-related statements and significantly negative sentiment in GenAI- and ethics-related statements, while student- and assessment-related statements do not differ significantly from neutral. Neither country nor the policy-dimension-by-country interaction is statistically significant. The interviews contextualize these policy-level patterns: participants described uncertainty around acceptable use, disclosure, and instructor expectations, with responses ranging from cautious experimentation to avoidance. Together, the findings show how differentiated GenAI guidance can coexist within university policy and illustrate the interpretive demands students may face when applying such guidance in practice. Clearer programme- and course-level guidance, consistent disclosure expectations, and stronger support for GenAI literacy may help connect institutional policy more closely with teaching and learning practice.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly central to innovation in small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), yet resource constraints limit their ability to exploit it. Governments worldwide provide institutional support to encourage SME AI adoption, but whether such support translates into innovation depends on internal organizational conditions that remain poorly understood. Drawing on institutional theory, this study treats government support as a source of coercive, normative, and mimetic pressure and develops an integrative conceptual model in which it influences SME innovation performance through AI adoption intensity, with organizational learning capability as a mediator and organizational readiness as a moderator. The model specifies that government support raises adoption intensity, which in turn enhances innovation performance; that organizational learning capability partially mediates this effect; and that organizational readiness strengthens the link between government support and adoption intensity. A quantitative, cross-sectional design is proposed: structured questionnaires will collect no fewer than 200 valid responses from SMEs, analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). Theoretically, the study is expected to extend institutional theory from the adoption/non-adoption dichotomy to a continuous adoption-intensity construct and to position organizational learning as the channel transmitting adoption into innovation. Practically, it can inform the design of differentiated government policy and SME capability building.

We present a graph-based framework for Composite AI systems that integrate multiple AI techniques to address complex problems. We describe an architecture using specialized control nodes to orchestrate diverse models including planning, machine learning, constraint programming, and large language models. The system employs directed acyclic graphs and behavior trees to manage model relationships and execution sequencing. Our methodology encompasses data connectors, computational services, and a containerized deployment framework supporting hierarchical, sequential, and concurrent model composition patterns. Through case studies, we demonstrate how this architecture enables the creation of composite systems that leverage the strengths of multiple AI techniques within a unified operational schema, overcoming the limitations of single-model approaches.

Geospatial pixel reasoning aims to generate segmentation masks in optical RGB remote sensing imagery directly from natural-language instructions. Most existing approaches fine-tune a multimodal large language models (MLLM) with dense pixel-level masks as ground truth. While effective within the training distribution, this paradigm suffers from two main drawbacks: (1) the high cost of large-scale dense mask annotation, and (2) the limited generalization capability of supervised fine-tuning (SFT) in out-of-domain (OOD) scenarios . To address these issues, we propose G eospatial pixel R easoning vi A S tructured P olicy learning ( GRASP ), a structured policy-learning framework that cascades an MLLM with a pretrained segmentation model. To enhance generalization, we introduce Pure Reinforcement for Instruction-to-Mask Execution ( PRIME ), a training paradigm that replaces SFT with reinforcement learning to better align reasoning and grounding behaviors with task objectives. To reduce annotation costs, we design Box-and-Points Rewards ( BoP-Rewards ), which substitute dense mask labels with bounding boxes and positive points. BoP-Rewards evaluate model outputs through two complementary signals: format, which constrains the reasoning and grounding structure to remain syntactically parsable, and accuracy, which measures the quality of predicted boxes and points. Our experiments focus on 3-channel optical RGB imagery from public remote sensing datasets. We train GRASP and all baselines on EarthReason and GeoPixInstruct, and construct an in-domain benchmark by merging their test sets. We further release GRASP -1k, a fully OOD benchmark with reasoning-intensive queries, reasoning traces, and fine-grained masks. Experimental results demonstrate state-of-the-art in-domain performance and a 54% relative improvement in OOD gIoU over GeoPix, the strongest competing baseline on this metric. These results confirm that reinforcement learning with cost-aware rewards provides a robust and scalable paradigm for geospatial pixel reasoning. All code and datasets will be released publicly.

Abstract—The exponential scaling of frontier Artificial Intelligence (AI) foundation models and global real-time inference workloads has precipitated an alarming surge in electrical energy consumption, water cooling demands, and greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. Training a single 70B+ parameter transformer model consumes hundreds of megawatt-hours (MWh) of electricity, while high-throughput inference serving clusters run continuous multi-kilowatt server racks across worldwide datacenters. In response, 'Green AI' has emerged as an essential computational discipline prioritizing energy efficiency, operational and embodied carbon footprint minimization, and computational sustainability alongside raw accuracy metrics ('Red AI'). However, transitioning enterprise computing systems toward sustainable AI introduces multifaceted engineering trade-offs: algorithmic compression vs. downstream reasoning degradation, non-uniform spatial-temporal grid carbon intensity, and memory bandwidth bottlenecks under low-precision quantization. This paper presents an exhaustive, mathematically formal technical survey and empirical architectural evaluation of Green AI spanning the entire lifecycle of foundation models. We formalize the holistic carbon accounting framework incorporating embodied silicon manufacturing emissions, model the mathematical dynamics of dynamic Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) token routing, analyze FlashAttention memory-IO energy bounds, and formulate carbon-aware spatiotemporal workload scheduling across geographically distributed datacenters. Furthermore, we construct an empirical enterprise benchmarking testbed across an 8-node NVIDIA H100/A100 cluster executing pre-training, fine-tuning, and inference on open foundation models (Llama-3-70B, Mixtral-8x7B). Our empirical findings demonstrate that sparse MoE routing paired with FP8 FlashAttention-3 slashes pre-training energy consumption by 48.2% while matching dense model perplexity. Concurrently, carbon-aware temporal job shifting achieves a 38.6% reduction in operational carbon dioxide equivalent (CO2e) emissions by aligning elastic training runs with regional renewable grid surpluses. Finally, we formulate open challenges in zero-water datacenter cooling, unified embodied carbon lifecycle tracking, and sustainable microarchitectural hardware co-design. Index Terms—Green AI, Sustainable Computing, Carbon Accounting, Mixture-of-Experts (MoE), FlashAttention, Speculative Decoding, Spatiotemporal Workload Scheduling, Energy-Efficient Deep Learning.

The explosive growth of the Internet of Things (IoT) has allowed connecting everywhere in the healthcare, smart city, agriculture, and industry areas. Nevertheless, the rapid increase in the launch of IoT ecosystem presents essential issues of data privacy, security, trust, and interoperability. The potential of blockchain technology to solve the problem has become one of the prospects of this technology, as it is decentralized, immutable, and transparent. However, traditional blockchain systems tend to be energy-intensive and computationally intensive, which makes them inappropriate in resource-limited IoT devices with low processing power, storage, and battery capacity. To address this shortcoming green blockchain models have been put forward, with the aim of ensuring energy efficiency, scalability, and sustainability without compromising on the strong security guarantees. This chapter offers an in-depth discussion on energy-efficient blockchain paradigms optimized to be used in IoT systems. It starts with the description of the inherent limitations of IoT devices and the inefficiency of classical consensus mechanisms of blockchains, including Proof-of-Work. The topic then focuses on the lightweight alternatives, such as hybrid consensus protocols, Proof-of-Stake, Delegated Proof-of-Stake, Proof-of-Authority, and ledgers based on Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs). The importance of edge and fog computing in minimizing the amount of energy spent on the execution of intensive blockchain tasks is also highlighted. Moreover, the chapter reviews real-life examples of green blockchain systems in the medical care monitoring, supply chain management, and smart city systems, in which sustainable and secure data management is essential. The main issues like interoperability within heterogeneous IoT platforms, decentralization versus energy saving trade-offs, and adherence to international sustainability objectives are reviewed critically. Lastly, the chapter also highlights potential research prospects in the future that involve artificial intelligence (AI)-based energy optimization capabilities, cross-chain interoperability systems, and how renewable energy sources can be incorporated into IoT deployments. This research integrates theoretical materials with real-life examples to support the idea of the transformative capability of green blockchain models in the development of IoT ecosystems to a new level of security, sustainability, and energy efficiency.

Abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence into environmental sustainability strategies presents a critical dilemma known as the "Green Tech Paradox." While AI offers unprecedented capabilities to optimize resource allocation, predict climate patterns, and enhance energy efficiency across industrial sectors, its deployment carries substantial, often overlooked, ecological costs. This research provides a critical analysis of the dual role AI plays as both a catalyst for eco-innovations and a significant contributor to environmental degradation. On the positive frontier, AI-driven applications accelerate sustainability by enabling smart power grids, improving carbon capture systems, facilitating precision agriculture, and modeling complex environmental crises. Machine learning algorithms enhance operational efficiency, reducing waste and carbon footprints in manufacturing and logistics. However, these beneficial outcomes are counterbalanced by the escalating physical footprint of AI infrastructure. The training and continuous execution of complex neural networks demand massive amounts of electricity, heavily relying on fossil-fuel-dominant energy grids. Furthermore, data centers consume millions of liters of freshwater daily for cooling mechanisms, accelerating localized water scarcity, while the rapid obsolescence of specialized hardware generates growing volumes of hazardous electronic waste. This paper evaluates this structural tension through a multidimensional synthesis of secondary data, life-cycle assessments, and resource consumption metrics across global data centers. The analysis reveals that without stringent regulatory frameworks and sustainable design interventions, the environmental degradation caused by AI's hardware lifecycle risks surpassing its ecological benefits. Ultimately, the study advocates for a paradigm shift toward "Green AI"—prioritizing algorithmic efficiency, renewable energy integration for computing infrastructure, sustainable hardware lifecycle management, and policy-driven eco-design standards. By establishing transparent auditing protocols, researchers and industry leaders can mitigate the hidden ecological liabilities of artificial intelligence, ensuring that modern technological advancement aligns genuinely with global net-zero targets and long-term planetary boundaries. Keywords: Green AI, Climate change mitigation, Sustainable development goals (SDGs), Environmental governance, Lifecycle assessment of AI.

Objectives: This study comprehensively investigates the underlying mechanisms through which green transformational leadership and work motivation influence sustainable employee performance. Specifically, the research evaluates the pivotal mediating role of employee engagement within the highly analytical and bureaucratic environment of Bank Indonesia, the nation's central bank. Methodology: We employed an explanatory quantitative research design utilizing a cross-sectional survey approach. The empirical data were collected from a carefully determined sample of 158 permanent employees across four strategic departments at Bank Indonesia using a stratified random sampling approach. To test the complex structural relationships and mediation effects, we applied Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) using the SmartPLS 4 software, executing a rigorous bootstrapping procedure with 5,000 subsamples. Finding: The empirical analysis reveals a compelling theoretical anomaly where green transformational leadership does not directly drive sustainable employee performance. Conversely, intrinsic work motivation exerts a strong, positive, and direct impact on the sustainability of employee performance. More importantly, both green leadership and work motivation are highly effective in cultivating deep employee engagement. Consequently, employee engagement emerges as a significant driver of sustainable performance, acting as a full mediator for green transformational leadership and a partial mediator for work motivation. Conclusion: Employee engagement functions as an absolute psychological bridge in a central banking context. Without this deep emotional and cognitive involvement, top-down environmental leadership visions and latent intrinsic motivation cannot effectively materialize into resilient, long-term sustainable performance.

Abstract Hera is an ESA contribution to the international planetary defense effort. It is a deep‐space mission to the binary asteroid system Didymos and Dimorphos, designed to investigate the effects of NASA's Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART), demonstrate autonomous navigation, and support close‐proximity investigation by two CubeSats. Hera includes a Spacecraft Monitoring Camera (SMC) for situational awareness during critical operations such as CubeSat deployments. Although not a science instrument, the SMC may also provide scientifically useful and outreach imagery. Integration was challenging because the SMC uses a private Packet Utilisation Standard (PUS) Type 210 service, was not modeled in the Hera spacecraft simulator, and was initially unsupported by the spacecraft Central Software (CSW). To enable early testing, a ground toolchain was developed for command generation, telemetry extraction, image reassembly, and PNG conversion. Without direct onboard support, commands and telemetry were encapsulated in PUS Service 2 packets, enabling test‐bench integration. Synthetic telemetry was used to validate the processing chain before restricted hardware access. Bench testing revealed a SpaceWire flow‐control anomaly that could stall the affected communication path, so planned SMC imaging during Hera's March 2025 Mars gravity‐assist flyby was canceled. The issue was subsequently addressed in a later flight‐software version, with cruise‐phase validation planned before asteroid proximity operations. This case shows how low‐level ground access, synthetic data, and staged testing can reduce the risk of deferring non‐launch‐critical onboard functionality until after launch.

Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have demonstrated promising capabilities for remote sensing reasoning, yet they frequently generate visually unsupported reasoning that contradicts the visual evidence. Existing post-training methods optimize primarily for final-answer correctness, providing limited supervision for identifying and correcting hallucinations that arise during the reasoning process. To address this limitation, we propose \textbf{FaithRS}, a hallucination-aware self-reflection framework for faithful reasoning in remote sensing. We first construct \textbf{SFHD-43K}, a dataset of 43K structured, fine-grained hallucination annotations, and train a detector to identify hallucination types, underlying causes, and supporting visual evidence. FaithRS then incorporates this diagnostic feedback into a Safe Detector-Guided Corrective Rollout framework, where a safety-aware gate selectively determines whether and how to revise the response. Training is driven by a composite reward that jointly optimizes answer accuracy, reasoning faithfulness, hallucination reduction, format compliance, and revision safety. Experiments with Qwen3.5 backbones (0.8B, 4B, and 9B) show consistent improvements across four remote sensing benchmarks, with gains of up to 11.64 points.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) has changed the dynamic of energy sustainability across the globe with regard to digital transformation. This chapter discusses AI and renewable energy systems convergence as the basis of smart, low-carbon societies. It discusses the ways in which machine learning, predictive analytics, and digital twins can be used to increase solar, wind, hydropower, bioenergy and geothermal resource forecasting, operational efficiency, fault detection and grid integration. The specific emphasis is put upon AI-driven solutions to intermittency, stabilizing smart grids, and optimizing energy distribution and demand management. The chapter, as well, assesses the increasing energy requirements of AI infrastructures and suggests ways of creating energy-efficient, low-carbon AI architectures. It combines the technical, environmental, and policy views to put the practical uses providing resilience and net-zero transitions and focus on governance, ethics, and responsible innovation to promote sustainable and inclusive development.

We introduce HelpMeOut, an embodied AI benchmark for error-aware monitoring of household task execution. Existing embodied household benchmarks typically assume that humans execute tasks correctly, but this assumption does not hold for cognitively impaired persons or older adults whose everyday activities produce structured execution errors. To address this gap, HelpMeOut operationalizes research on everyday action errors into 20000 paired activity episodes, covering nine neuropsychologically motivated error categories. In each episode, agents observe a streaming human activity trajectory and must monitor whether the execution is unfolding correctly, diagnosing any structured errors as early as possible. We evaluate learned-monitor, symbolic, change-point, and frontier LLM prompting baselines. Results show that these methods perform poorly as error monitors, often missing when execution goes wrong. These results suggest a gap left by standard goal-inference and task-completion benchmarks, making HelpMeOut a testbed for error-aware assistive agents.

Hemolytic illness, an immune-mediated disease that can be fatal, is brought on by maternal alloantibodies against fetal red blood cell antigens inherited from the father. Fetal anemia, hyperbilirubinemia, hydrops fetalis, and, in extreme circumstances, perinatal mortality these placental-crossing maternal immunoglobulin G antibodies. The incidence of RhD linked HDFN has decreased significantly, however alloimmunization against other blood group antigens such Kell, Rh c, Rh E, Duffy, Kidd, and ABO antigens still causes clinically significant disease. Thus, HDFN remains a significant concern in the fields of immunohematology, transfusion medicine, obstetrics, and neonatology. This review aims to present the current knowledge of the immunohematological mechanism of maternal alloimmunization and fetal hemolysis, especially focusing on clinically important blood group systems and antibody characteristics. Recent prenatal diagnostic developments, There have been notable advancements in early diagnosis and risk stratification of affected pregnancies because of advancements in technology like MCA-PSV Doppler ultrasound, molecular immunohematology, high throughput genotyping, and cell-free fetal DNA for non-invasive fetal blood type genotyping. Newer management techniques, including serial maternal antibody monitoring, intrauterine transfusion, optimized timing of delivery, neonatal phototherapy, exchange transfusion and evidence-based transfusion support, have dramatically improved the survival of fetuses and minimized disease-related complications. In addition, new technologies and innovations such as those based on artificial intelligence that can predict risk, digital immunohematology, automated compatibility testing, FcRn inhibitors, complement targeted therapies, and personalized immunotherapeutic strategies will help further define the diagnosis and management of HDFN. Nevertheless, the world faces many obstacles to achieving these advances, including the lack of access to molecular diagnostics, availability of appropriate blood products, and unequal distribution of health care services. Further multidisciplinary teamwork, technological innovations, and standardized clinical approaches will play a key role in furthering the goals of precision medicine and improving maternal and neonatal outcomes in the management of HDFN.

With the acceleration of urbanization, urban public safety risks have exhibited characteristics of diversification, complexity, and linkage. Based on the grid-based governance concept of “comprehensive horizontal coverage and hierarchical vertical stratification” and combined with the hierarchical DEMATEL method, this paper constructs an urban public safety Grid Risk System for Urban Public Safety (GRSFUPS) and a risk analysis framework. GRSFUPS takes grids as the minimum governance units and progressively refines four types of A-level risks—natural disasters, public health, social security, and accident disasters—into B-level and C-level risks, forming a complex system with clear hierarchies and close linkages. Subsequently, using Kunming as a case study, a case application study was conducted on its critical public safety risks. Combined with centrality ranking and the Pareto principle, 55 critical risk factors were identified from 258 risk factors. Research results indicate that public health incidents and accident disaster risks occupy a dominant position in Kunming City, while natural disaster risks such as meteorological and flood hazards repeatedly appear across multiple districts and exhibit significant amplification effects. Theoretically, this paper enriches the urban public safety risk identification framework from a grid-based perspective. Practically, it provides a new analytical paradigm and methodological support for Kunming City and other similar cities to conduct risk governance under grid-based management models.

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for UI/UX evaluation and design decision support; however, their responses are often generated as implicit and unstructured outputs, making cognitive processes and judgment rationale difficult to trace. Moreover, the quality of LLM-based judgments may vary depending on users’ prompting proficiency, limiting the consistency of AI-assisted evaluation. This study proposes HIPA (Human Information Processing Architecture), a cognitive response architecture that structures LLM outputs based on the human information processing (HIP) model and investigates the manifestation of human cognitive stages in conventional LLM responses. HIPA maps four HIP stages—perception, working memory, decision making, and response execution—into a two-stage response structure consisting of information provision and judgment support through knowledge-grounded prompting with GPT-4o. An exploratory evaluation was conducted with seven participants with different prompting proficiency levels who assessed the same mobile login interface using a general LLM. Responses were coded according to HIP-stage manifestation using a three-point scale. The results showed that perception and response execution were consistently observed, whereas working memory and decision-making stages varied depending on prompt systematicity. These findings indicate that general LLM responses do not inherently provide cognitively structured judgment support. HIPA provides a human-centered framework for developing AI-assisted UI/UX evaluation systems based on human cognitive principles.

Human factors and ergonomics (HFE) is vital for optimising human-centred system design. This study aimed to synthesise research on HFE and examine its historical evolution, current landscape and emerging trends. A bibliometric analysis and a knowledge-domain mapping analysis were conducted to combine perspectives on journal development and article output. This study focused on 24 journals classified in the ergonomics category in the Journal Citation Reports of 2024. Critical information for the 24 HFE journals was investigated, including commencement year of publication, composition of editorial boards, number of published papers, publishing models, 2024 quartile rankings and impact factors and 5-year impact factors. Two visualisation tools, VOSviewer and CiteSpace, were used to perform the bibliometric analysis of the 26,026 HFE documents in the Web of Science Core Collection, spanning 2010 to 2024. Results showed that HFE literature has evolved from classical industrial origins to modern technological paradigms. Increased collaborations across different research areas to address HFE problems were observed. The review also identified key domain expansions across high-impact emerging HFE frontiers, including artificial intelligence, extended reality, autonomous vehicles and wearable technologies. Building upon these findings, the study may provide in-depth insights into the critical future HFE research directions.

While AI agents are useful for many tasks, they regularly misbehave in destructive ways, such as deleting important data. While prior work has focused on preventing such misbehavior, we consider how to recover after an agent misbehaves. We propose verifiable agent insurance (VAI), a framework for agent providers to commit financially to promises, a list of programmatically-specified policies that an agent is meant to follow. These promises are embedded in a smart contract on an immutable ledger (e.g., a blockchain) to prevent tampering, along with a monetary escrow. A user who detects a violation of committed promises can prompt a verifier to review agent execution traces, which are logged through the agent harness's shared tool-execution path, without instrumenting each tool separately. Upon verification of the violation, the agent provider's escrow funds are paid to the reporting user. We instantiate VAI as an end-to-end implementation on an Ethereum layer-2 network, and evaluate its coverage on three prominent agent benchmarks, two of which we re-annotated to obtain task-level policy-compliance labels. Currently, many agents do not emit user authorizations and security-relevant information as explicit, structured data objects -- rather, they embed the data needed to verify policy violations in natural language exchanges. Even so, VAI manages to detect violations in 42.2% of runs containing violations across three benchmarks. By augmenting agents to explicitly emit such objects, violation detection rises to 83.0% of traces. Our findings suggest that for improved auditability, agents should be co-designed with their security policies to emit explicit, structured records of user authorization and security-relevant actions.

Purpose Based on the self-determination theory, this study aims to examine the mechanisms and boundary conditions through which the use of artificial intelligence sales technology (AIST) shapes sales performance. Design/methodology/approach Study 1 conducted a questionnaire survey of 396 sales employees and their supervisors in China’s real estate industry. Study 2 adopted a time-lagged research design involving 324 sales employees in various industries and their immediate supervisors. Regression analyses with Mplus 8.3 were performed to test the hypotheses. Findings The empirical results indicate that the use of AIST indirectly influences sales performance through the mediating roles of the satisfaction of three basic psychological needs – autonomy, competence and relatedness. Furthermore, salespeople’s performance goal orientation attenuates the positive relationship between AIST usage and the satisfaction of salespeople’s needs for competence and relatedness. Originality/value This study advances the emerging literature on the effectiveness of AIST usage by revealing the psychological pathways through which AIST influences sales performance and offers practical insights for strengthening AI–human collaboration in the workplace.

ABSTRACT Artificial intelligence is increasingly embedded in socially interactive roles, with virtual influencers emerging as a prominent form of AI‐mediated communication. This study examines how consumers engage with agents that simulate social presence yet lack independent agency. Using a mixed‐methods design, we investigate how authenticity, transparency, and privacy concerns relate to trust, acceptance, and responsibility attribution. The findings show that consumer responses cannot be reduced to trust formation alone. Instead, individuals evaluate whether engagement remains acceptable under conditions of artificial agency. Authenticity supports trust by providing coherence, while transparency and privacy concerns introduce competing interpretations related to control and risk. Privacy concerns are also associated with greater responsibility attribution to brands and developers. These results suggest that engagement with virtual influencers can be interpreted as a process in which consumers negotiate trust and accountability. The study offers an integrated perspective on AI‐mediated influence and highlights the role of distributed responsibility in shaping consumer responses.
topics: Consumer Behavior in Brand Consumption and Identification

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) presents an opportunity to transform neonatal care. By rapidly assimilating large volumes of complex, multi-dimensional data to produce real-time predictions, machine learning (ML) models have the potential to enable personalised monitoring and treatment and earlier intervention. This narrative review aims to provide clinicians with a foundational overview of AI and its potential role in the care of preterm infants, with a particular focus on respiratory pathologies. We introduce different types of AI tools and ways to assess predictive model performance. We summarise existing literature using AI and conventional predictive models to predict respiratory conditions, including extubation readiness, bronchopulmonary dysplasia, and apnoea occurrence and risk. Finally, we discuss current limitations of AI in neonatology, barriers to clinical translation and the next steps needed to overcome them. These may include multicentre collaboration and data sharing, using dynamic inputs such as vital signs to reflect evolving physiology, and improved transparency, accessibility and training for clinicians, as well as clear guidelines for clinical application, accountability and ongoing monitoring.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: BackgroundAutomation, including both robots and AI, are increasingly implemented in the public sector to handle an increased demand for services while facing a shortage of staff. However, little is known of how automation is related to employees' work characteristics and well-being.ObjectiveThe purpose of the present study was to examine how automation is related to work characteristics and well-being in a national sample of social workers.MethodsA cross-sectional survey was conducted with a sample of 1428 social workers in Sweden, comparing those working with automation technologies (e.g., robotization in terms of automated decision-making support in financial aid) to those without.ResultsThe findings indicate that automation is negatively related to relational aspects of work, such as beneficiary contact and social support, and increases perceived workload and role conflict. However, no significant differences were found on decision-making autonomy, role clarity, or skill variety. Despite these work design changes, no significant differences in well-being outcomes, such as burnout and vigor, were observed between the two groups.ConclusionThe findings suggest that automation may alter the nature of social work without necessarily changing employee well-being. These insights have implications for organizations seeking to implement automation in a way that supports employees' work experience and well-being.

People increasingly bring their health questions to ChatGPT, yet safety evaluations of LLM health advice rest almost entirely on clinician-authored vignettes, synthetic prompts, or simulated user profiles. The gap is widest for the Global South, where concerns about demographic bias and unsafe recommendations are well documented but have never been tested on real usage. We present, to our knowledge, the first demographically grounded safety evaluation of real-world health conversations with ChatGPT. From a consent-based data-donation corpus of 202,590 conversations from 1,252 users in India, Nigeria, Brazil, and Pakistan (December 2022 to February 2026), each linked to self-reported age and gender, we identify 15,555 health conversations, classify their health intent using an LLM classifier adapted from an established taxonomy, and score response safety under both a context-blind and a user-context-aware rubric. Roughly one in five health conversations receives a high-risk rating. Risk concentrates in symptom and condition queries and recurs through identifiable failure modes: unsafe medication or dosage guidance, harmful self-diagnosis, missing safety warnings, encouraging over-reliance on the model, and failure to refer users to professionals. Supplying the user's own accumulated context raises the high-risk share by 13-17 percentage points, and about one in four conversations rated safe in isolation turns out to be unsafe for the specific person asking. Safety evaluations built on synthetic cases are likely to miss these harms.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Abstract Pfeffer, Krügel, and Uhl (2025) report that OpenAI’s reasoning model o1-mini produces more utilitarian responses to the trolley problem and footbridge dilemma than the non-reasoning model GPT-4o, and they raise the question whether growing reasoning capabilities bring about a “utilitarian turn” in LLMs. I extend their exploratory study in a direction they call for: with four current OpenAI models and systematic prompt variation. On the trolley dilemma, the hypothesized utilitarian turn is not confirmed. GPT-4o’s low utilitarian rate reflects safety refusals triggered by the prompt’s advisory framing rather than a deontological commitment; on reformulated prompt variants—for instance, agent-neutral “Is it morally permissible…?” instead of advisory “Should I…?”—all four models, reasoning or not, converge on utilitarian answers. The footbridge finding is partially confirmed: reasoning models tend to give more utilitarian responses than non-reasoning models across prompt variations, but they often refuse to answer or answer non-utilitarian. These results demonstrate that single-prompt evaluations of LLM moral responses are unreliable: multi-prompt robustness testing should be standard practice for any empirical claims about LLM behavior.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI
Psychology of Moral and Emotional Judgment

documents.abstract: The innovation ecosystem is expressed in the form of a network system that plays an important role in the economic development of countries in the 21st century.It is necessary to consider the innovation ecosystem in a way as an innovative environment in creation of which all sides implementing innovative work and service processes-governmental and non-governmental organizations, commercial associations and, most importantly, human capital are involved.Human capital, which refers to the skills, knowledge, experience and creativity of individuals within society, is a key driver of innovation and a fundamental element in fostering a dinamic and sustainable innovation ecosystem.The human factor encourages the generation of ideas, entrepreneurship, collaboration and knowledge creation, contributing to the development of innovative solutions and the economic and social progress of a region or country.The research study investigated the role and importance of human capital in the innovation ecosystem, which is a particularly important factor in the modern world of information and digitization, where the main focus is on the "brain product".The result of researchers who have studied the mentioned topic before, are analyzed during the research, and the statistical data is used as the main data supporting the hypothesis.

The purpose of the research -This article examines human capital assessment through the integration of heterogeneous data and artificial intelligence in the context of the digital economy.The study aims to identify the interrelationships among artificial intelligence, digital transformation, and human capital, and to empirically evaluate how these factors influence productivity. Research methodology -The research applies analysis, comparison, systematization, grouping, and generalization methods.Its empirical part is based on panel data covering the period 2010-2024 and obtained from open international statistical databases.The analytical framework includes descriptive statistics, correlation analysis, unit root tests, cointegration analysis, multivariate regression modeling, and Granger causality testing.This methodological approach allows a comprehensive assessment of the interaction between artificial intelligence, digital transformation, human capital, and productivity.Results of the research -The findings show that artificial intelligence has a significant positive impact on productivity, while human capital strongly reinforces this effect.Digital transformation also contributes positively through better data processing and resource allocation.The results confirm long-run relationships among the variables and identify artificial intelligence and human capital as major drivers of productivity growth.Originality and scientific novelty of the research -The study offers an integrated and multidimensional framework for evaluating human capital in the digital economy.

This article presents a systematic literature review of the role of human capital in digital transformation and artificial intelligence (AI), focusing on how these developments reshape workforce competencies and human resource management (HRM) during the transition from Industry 4.0 to Industry 5.0. Following the PRISMA guidelines, the study combines thematic coding with comparative analysis. From an initial pool of 216 publications, 46 studies were selected for in-depth analysis. The review examines how AI and digitalisation change workforce skill requirements and how HRM mechanisms can help organisations develop and sustain the necessary competencies. The findings indicate a shift from routine and manual tasks toward hybrid competency profiles that integrate data analytics skills, AI literacy, human–machine interaction skills, and higher-order socio-cognitive capabilities, including adaptive reasoning, collaboration, and ethical judgement. HRM emerges as a strategic integrator that supports continuous reskilling, predictive skills-gap analysis, and the development of effective human–AI teams. Based on these findings, the study proposes a multilevel framework explaining how institutional mechanisms, organisational strategy, HRM practices, and human–AI complementarity jointly shape workforce competitiveness in AI-enabled digital transformation. The framework contributes to human-centric digitalisation by linking workforce competitiveness to capability velocity and human–AI complementarity. It also provides managerial implications for designing learning, governance, and decision-making structures that enable organisations to respond to evolving competency requirements and translate technological potential into sustainable operational advantages.

Service organizations increasingly employ artificial intelligence and predictive analytics to allocate financial, technological, workforce, and operational resources. Although algorithmic systems can process complex organizational data, purely prediction-driven approaches may generate recommendations that are difficult for managers to interpret, validate, or reconcile with organizational constraints. These limitations become particularly important in healthcare and other information-intensive service environments where resource allocation decisions interact with workforce capacity, digital workflows, privacy requirements, project priorities, and service quality objectives. This study proposes a human centered explainable artificial intelligence framework for adaptive resource allocation and decision governance. The framework integrates predictive modeling, multi objective optimization, and explainability mechanisms within a structured decision support architecture. Rather than optimizing a single performance measure, the proposed approach considers multiple objectives including operational efficiency, resource utilization, service responsiveness, workforce capacity, fairness, and decision transparency. A human-in-the-loop governance mechanism allows decision-makers to review explanations, modify organizational constraints, and evaluate alternative allocation scenarios before recommendations are implemented. Because real organizational data are not used in the present study, the framework is evaluated using synthetically generated operational environments representing variations in demand, workforce availability, resource limitations, project priorities, and unexpected disruptions. Scenario and sensitivity analyses can then examine how resource allocation recommendations change under alternative organizational conditions. The principal contribution is an integrated analytical architecture in which optimization and explainability operate as complementary components of organizational decision making. The proposed framework can provide a foundation for transparent resource allocation systems applicable to healthcare, professional services, digital enterprises, and other service-oriented organizations seeking to improve efficiency and resilience while retaining managerial oversight.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society
